description: Sensata Technologies Holding plc develops, manufactures, and sells sensors and sensor-rich solutions, electrical protection components and systems, and other products used in mission-critical systems
description_full: Sensata Technologies Holding plc develops, manufactures, and sells sensors and sensor-rich solutions, electrical protection components and systems, and other products used in mission-critical systems and applications in the United States, Europe, Asia, and internationally. It operates through three segments: Automotive; Industrials; and Aerospace, Defense, and Commercial Equipment. The company offers sensors, contactors/fuses, switching and protection devices and solutions, distribution modules, bimetal electromechanical controls, circuit breakers, switches and relays, energy storage systems, rectifiers and frequency converters, power conversion systems, battery management system, charging inlet modules, and brushless DC motors. It offers its products for thermal management and air conditioning systems; powertrain; exhaust after-treatment; suspension, braking; tire management solutions; battery packs; electrical protection; electrical powertrain; battery packs; charging systems; motors, compressors, pumps; heating and cooling systems; home appliances; lighting; industrial; data and telecom equipment; medical equipment; motors, compressors, and pumps; hydraulic machinery; motion control systems; motor/platform controllers; grid harmonics and power delivery; commercial and military aircraft; and recreational vehicles. It serves automotive, on-road truck, and construction; and original equipment manufacturers in agriculture, control, appliance, medical, energy and charging infrastructure, data/telecom, and aerospace and defense industries, as well as systems integrators, aerospace, and motor and compressor distributors. Sensata Technologies Holding plc was founded in 1916 and is headquartered in Attleboro, Massachusetts.
ceo_bio: Mr. Stephan  Von Schuckmann | CEO & Director | Age 51 | Compensation: $5.2M (FY2025)
culture_narrative: Employs approximately 16K people. Revenue per employee of $222K ranks in the bottom quartile among Technology peers, improving at 5%/yr — growing workforce leverage. Each employee generates $29K of free cash flow annually. Stock-based compensation of $1K per employee reflects an ownership culture. CEO compensation is 24× revenue per employee (reasonable relative to workforce productivity). Governance score flags low compensation governance risk (1/10).
financial_summary: Sensata Technologies Holding pl is a mid-cap technology business with a $5.7B market cap on $3.7B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at -3% over the past three years and +2% annually across the full decade, and a shrinking top line is the hardest headwind any business can overcome.
Returns on capital run at 2% against a 8% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests.

The business throws off $490M in free cash flow — roughly 13 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 19.86× so those profits are backed by real cash.
Accruals are elevated at -8.7% of assets, and Sloan showed firms building earnings through accruals rather than cash systematically underperform.
On the balance sheet, debt is heavy at 4.6× net debt/EBITDA, and leverage like that is what turns a bad year into a permanent loss, and thin 1.6× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.

Shareholder yield of 3.3% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and profit capture is only 0.3× the fair share, suggesting no structural edge inside its industry.

sect: Its 6% operating margin is roughly in line with the Technology median (7%).
It captures well under its share of sector profits (0.27x its revenue share).
Over five years it has been losing share of the sector profit pool (-20.2% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 530 companies in the universe; the top four hold 29% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 45% over the past year excluding the latest month, though it has pulled back 17% over the last three months.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 27% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 40% and a beta of 1.17, it moves roughly with the market.
About $53.4M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 57% in the 2020 crash and 42% in the 2022 bear market.
val: The stock trades 38% below its DCF fair value of $63.31, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 17%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $42.58 to $95.78 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks cheap against Technology peers: P/E 15.7 vs 26.7, EV/EBITDA 9.2 vs 16.4 and P/FCF 11.7 vs 25.4 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 77% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are mixed: an FCF yield of 8.6% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 3.2% (vs the 8% bar).
The 10 covering analysts target $52.80 on average, 34% above the price.
prof: ROIC of 2% falls short of the cost of capital of 8.0%, so growth at these returns destroys value; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.49).
It converts 13% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality is a concern: high accruals (-8.7% of assets).
ROE of 1% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (2.4x equity multiplier).
It spends 3.6% of revenue on R&D and 0.7% on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is heavy at 4.6x net debt to EBITDA ($573.0M of cash against $2.8B of debt), and interest cover is thin at 1.6x.
Goodwill makes up 47% of assets, a soft asset exposed to impairment.
growth: Revenue has compounded at -2.8% over 3 years, 4.0% over 5 years and 2.2% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating.
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Free cash flow has compounded 1.6% a year over five years, short of the 5% durability bar.
Capex runs only 0.5x depreciation (3.5% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
Its Rule of 40 score is 17, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
It has beaten earnings estimates by 7.0% on average.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.8%), and reported institutional holdings exceed 100% of shares (a sign of heavy share lending).
It returns 3.3% a year to shareholders (2.1% in buybacks and 1.2% in dividends).
The share count has shrunk 0.8% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
people: With about 16,700 employees, each generates about $222K of revenue, 0.6x the Technology median, and productivity has risen 5.2% a year.
That works out to $29K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $5.2M (24x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (1/10, lower is better).
